n: The narrator lists the nations God left in Canaan. They would test the new generation that had not lived through Joshua’s wars.
A second purpose: each generation had to learn for itself how to fight and trust God. Faith cannot simply be inherited.

f.g: To give them their own experience of relying on God in conflict.

n: The remaining peoples: the five Philistine city-states on the coast, Canaanites, Sidonians (Phoenicians), and Hivites in the far north.

f.g: Rulers of Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, Ekron and Gath.
A pass in Syria marking the far northern limit of the promised land.

n: The test was obedience: would Israel listen to the commandments given through Moses?

f.w: to know whether they would hearken

n: Israel settles in among six Canaanite peoples instead of standing apart.
Intermarriage leads to idolatry — exactly what Moses and Joshua had warned would happen.
Israel forgets the Lord and worships Baals and Asherah poles. “Forgat” is the key word: neglect, not just rebellion, begins apostasy.

f.g: Forgot.
Hebrew asheroth: sacred wooden poles or images of the goddess Asherah, not literal tree groves.

n: God hands Israel to Cushan-rishathaim, whose name means “Cushan of double wickedness” — perhaps a mocking nickname. Israel serves him eight years.

f.g: “Doubly wicked Cushan,” likely a play on his name.
Hebrew Aram-naharaim, “Aram of the two rivers,” in northern Mesopotamia.

n: Israel cries out, and the Lord raises up Othniel, Caleb’s kinsman, as the first judge. His brief story is the model the others are measured against.
The Spirit of the Lord comes on Othniel, empowering him to lead and win. Deliverance comes by God’s Spirit, not mere human talent.

f.w: the Spirit of the LORD came upon him

n: Forty years of peace follow — about a generation.

f.g: A round number often meaning a full generation.

n: Israel sins again, and God strengthens Eglon of Moab against them. Even a foreign king can be God’s instrument of discipline.

f.g: His name may suggest “young bull” or “calf”; the story uses it with irony.

n: Eglon allies with Ammon and Amalek, defeats Israel, and takes Jericho — “the city of palm trees.”

f.g: Jericho, or its site.

n: Israel serves Moab eighteen years, sending regular tribute.

f.g: Paid tribute and lived under their rule.

n: God raises up Ehud, a left-handed Benjamite. Ironically, Benjamin means “son of the right hand.” Ehud carries Israel’s tribute to Eglon.

f.g: Literally “bound in his right hand”; Benjamin was known for left-handed warriors.
Tribute payment.

n: Ehud makes a short two-edged dagger, about eighteen inches, and straps it to his right thigh, where guards checking a right-handed man would not look.

f.g: About 18 inches (45 cm); here possibly a shorter cubit.
Clothing.

n: Ehud delivers the tribute. The note that Eglon was very fat sets up what follows.

f.g: The Hebrew word plays on “fatling,” fitting the calf pun on his name.

n: After the tribute is delivered, Ehud sends the carriers away.

f.g: Carried.

n: Turning back at the stone images near Gilgal, Ehud returns alone and asks for a private audience. Eglon sends everyone out.

f.g: Possibly “carved images” or idols — boundary markers near Gilgal.
An order to the attendants: “Quiet!” or “Leave us.”

n: Eglon sits alone in his cool upper room. When Ehud says he has a message from God, Eglon rises — out of respect or curiosity.

f.g: A cool upper chamber on the roof.
Hebrew davar can mean both “word” and “thing,” a grim double meaning.

n: Using his left hand, Ehud draws the hidden dagger and strikes.
The vivid detail stresses how completely the oppressor fell. The story is told with the earthy humor of an oppressed people.

f.g: Handle.

n: Ehud leaves, locking the doors behind him, and slips away.

f.g: Possibly a vestibule or an opening; the Hebrew word is rare.

n: The servants find the doors locked and assume the king is relieving himself — giving Ehud time to escape.

f.g: A polite way of saying “relieving himself.”

n: They wait until embarrassed, then unlock the doors and find their king dead.

f.g: Waited until they were uneasy or embarrassed.

n: Ehud escapes past the stone images to Seirath in the hills.

f.g: A place in Ephraim’s hill country; location uncertain.

n: In the hills of Ephraim he sounds the trumpet, and Israel rallies to follow him.

f.g: A ram’s horn (shofar) calling men to battle.

n: Ehud credits the Lord with the victory. Israel seizes the Jordan crossings, trapping the Moabite forces west of the river.
About ten thousand strong, well-fed Moabite soldiers fall, with none escaping.

f.g: Robust, sturdy (another wordplay on “fat”).

n: Moab is humbled and the land enjoys eighty years of rest — the longest peace in Judges.

f.g: Eighty.

n: A brief note on Shamgar, who killed six hundred Philistines with an ox-goad, a long pointed farm stick. God can use humble tools. “Son of Anath” may suggest a non-Israelite background.

f.g: A long wooden pole, often with a metal tip, for driving oxen.
